ACUCOBOL-GT reserved words: fetched the WebWorks page manifest for book 4 of the v9.0.1 documentation set (gtman4/wwhdata/common/files.js), which names gt4b3.htm as 'B.2 Reserved Word List', fetched that page with curl, and took every

or

paragraph inside the B.2 body (from the first

onward). Most letters are tabulated two-up in pCellBody cells; the short letter groups (J, K, Q, V, Y, Z) are plain pBody paragraphs, and missing that second class silently drops 14 words, so both are read. Each cell is stripped of tags, HTML-unescaped, NBSP-normalised and matched against ^([A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(-[A-Z0-9]+)*)(\(markers\))?$; single letters are the alphabet headings and are discarded. Exactly two cells fail that match, 'DATE YYYYMMDD(a)' and 'DAY YYYYDDD(a)' -- see notes. Cross-checked by a completely separate extraction of the v8.1.3 Appendices PDF (pdftotext -raw, PDF pages 33-48 = Appendix B): 597 words shared, 0 words only in the PDF, 0 marker disagreements; the one difference, ENTRY, is the PDF printing its markers as '(a, b)' with a space so the tokeniser split it. ACUCOBOL-GT intrinsic functions: the Appendix F.2.1 table (gt4f4.htm) read the same way, cross-checked against the 'F.n Function' section titles in files.js and against the same headings in the v8.1.3 PDF -- all three agree on the same 43 rows / 44 names (ABSOLUTE-VALUE is printed as 'ABSOLUTE-VALUE (or ABS)'). ACUCOBOL-GT registers and system-names: grepped the v8.1.3 Reference Manual text (pdftotext -layout) for ' special register' and read the SPECIAL-NAMES syntax rules at 4-6..4-17. RM/COBOL: pdftotext the v12 LRM twice. -layout for the Appendix A reserved-word grid (PDF pages 489-496), because -layout keeps the space between a word and its superscript footnote digit ('COMP-4 1', 'DEBUG-SUB-1 1') whereas -raw glues it into the word ('COMP-41', 'DEBUG-SUB-11'); a bare '1' token is therefore attached to the preceding word as the footnote marker. -raw for Table 37 (context-sensitive words) and Tables 38-42 (nonreserved system-names), whose left column -layout smears across misaligned rows. Special Symbols (page 498) are punctuation, not words, and were skipped. The fifteen special registers are the ones the manual names in Chapter 1 under 'Special Registers'; the count matches the manual's own 'fifteen special registers are described below'. Cross-checked against the Liant v8.0 LRM Appendix A grid (pages 523-528): 402 words, all 402 also in v12, 0 conflicts, 0 marker disagreements; v12 adds exactly AS, IMP and the seven later special registers. Independent consistency test across the two products: of the 29 ACUCOBOL words marked (r) 'reserved by both ACUCOBOL-GT and RM/COBOL', 26 are in RM/COBOL v12's own list (EOL and EOS as context-sensitive words); the 4 absent ones -- EXTENDED-SEARCH, FILE-LIMIT, FILE-LIMITS, SEEK -- are RM/COBOL-74-era words no longer in v12, which is what one would expect, and none of them is a spelling variant of an RM/COBOL word.

curl through Bash for every byte, then local parsing; no word was typed from memory. Nothing GnuCOBOL-derived was opened (see notes). Function-names" and each section's elements taken; inner
separators are split on (three elements hold two words each, e.g. COMMIT
COMMON, which a naive strip silently concatenates). Leading "*" (DML-only) and "#" (dropped under ENABLE-KEYWORDS=*COBOL85) markers are stripped; the 11 operator glyphs (< <= + * ** - / > >= : =) are dropped. Every one of the 504 words was then re-found in the independently downloaded full COBOL2000 PDF, which is how the three concatenations were caught. NetCOBOL and Bull GCOS 7: their appendices carry per-word marker columns, and in BOTH the flat pdftotext layer misaligns those columns against the word column, so the markers were read positionally from pymupdf word boxes instead. NetCOBOL Appendix A (PDF pages 684-704): word column x0~100, five NetCOBOL platform columns at x~226/250/275/299/324, two standards-reference columns at x~369/413, Remarks asterisk at x~458; a word is kept when it carries an "o" in a NetCOBOL column. Two rows are hyphen-wrapped across printed lines and were stitched (DB-ACCESS-CONTROL-KEY, MULTICONVERSATION-MODE). Bull Appendix A (PDF pages 613-626, printed A-3..A-16): word column x~130, col.1 (DPS7 or a note ref) x~310, DSA x~369, ANSI x~425, JOD|SBS x~483; words are then bucketed by the appendix's own legend - DPS7 -> reserved, notes (2)(4)(5) -> DML-only reserved, note (8) -> function, notes (3)(1)(7)-device -> systemName, note (7)-other and JOD/SBS-only -> excluded. gap-adjudicate.title: Adjudication of the 21 residue words against the first pass's 230-file corpus plus newly searched vendor documentation. Documents relied on: ACUCOBOL-GT 8.1.3 User Interface Programming, 8.1.3 Reference Manual, 8.1.3 Appendices and 9.0.1 Appendices Appendix B.2 Reserved Word List; Heirloom Computing Elastic COBOL Language Reference Manual Appendix (August 2012); Micro Focus Visual COBOL 9.0 Reserved Words Table and Context-sensitive Words Table; IBM Enterprise COBOL for z/OS 6.4 'Reserved words'; IBM COBOL for VSE/ESA Language Reference SC26-8073-02 Table 48; Veryant isCOBOL Evolve 2021R2 Appendix D 'Intrinsic Functions' and isCOBOL Evolve 2023 R1 Overview; RM/COBOL Language Reference Manual, Second Edition (Version 12, Liant Software); Unisys COBOL ANSI-85 Programming Reference Manual Vol.1 (86001518-307); ISO/IEC 1989:20xx CD 1.2 (2009-08-23); COBOL Consortium (Japan) summary of ISO/IEC 1989:2023

gap-adjudicate.method: 1. Rendered every fetched PDF that lacked a text sibling with 'pdftotext -layout' into words/pdftxt (31 new renderings), giving a searchable corpus of 230 text files across src/, src2/ and pdftxt/; without this step 31 of the 45 PDFs, including the Heirloom, Unisys, IBM VSE and Veryant release-note documents that carry the decisive evidence, would have gone unsearched. 2. Exact scan (bin/adj_scan.py): each of the 21 words as a case-insensitive whole token with hyphen-aware boundaries, (?<![A-Za-z0-9_-])WORD(?![A-Za-z0-9_-]). Result: 20 of the 21 have zero occurrences anywhere in the corpus; only LOW-COLOR occurs (17 hits), plus a single CONTENT-LENGTH hit that proved on inspection to be an HTTP header. 3. Near-miss probe (bin/adj_near.py): for each word a relaxed pattern allowing an optional hyphen or space at each internal boundary, for example DOT[- ]?DASH, \bNO[- ]?TAB\b, BINARY[- ]?C[- ]?LONG, UN[- ]?S?EQUAL, AREA[- ]?VALUES?, (BITMAP[- ]?)?TRANSPARENT[- ]?COLOU?R. This separates genuine absence both from pdftotext column splitting and from variant spellings, and it is what surfaced DOT-DASH, NO-TAB, TRANSPARENT-COLOR, AREA-VALUE, METACLASS, EGCS and UNEQUAL as the real words behind seven of the entries. Every near-hit was then read with surrounding lines and classified as word table, syntax format, example text, or running prose. 4. Cross-checked each candidate against the vendors' own word tables, parsed rather than eyeballed: ACUCOBOL-GT 9.0.1 Appendix B.2 (624 distinct words extracted), Micro Focus Visual COBOL 9.0 Reserved Words and Context-sensitive Words Tables, IBM Enterprise COBOL 6.4 reserved words, IBM COBOL for VSE/ESA Table 48, and Veryant isCOBOL Appendix D (all 66 function names extracted from the HTML table rows). 5. WebSearch against primary vendor documentation for every word still unresolved, and a direct fetch of the one independent-vendor function list that searches suggested (TmaxSoft OpenFrame; DNS did not resolve, so it contributed nothing either way). 6. Self-check: re-extracted the PDFs with 'pdftotext -raw', a different extraction mode from the -layout text used for scanning, and confirmed each load-bearing string independently of the renderings the judgements were made on.

gap-fujitsu-ibm.method: 1. Read each of the 34 located words out of the file already identified for it, then judged it by what the document is doing where the word appears. Every candidate was searched all-caps and word-bounded (negative lookbehind and lookahead on [A-Za-z0-9-]) over the whole document, never case-insensitively, because most of these candidates are ordinary English words in prose and several are fragments of longer tokens.2. Built a negative check per family: IBM's 'Reserved words' appendix parsed by taking column 0 of each <tr> only - columns 2-4 hold 'X' marks, which is what makes a naive cell scan report 'X' as a word - giving 515 words; NetCOBOL V11 Appendix A 'List of Reserved Words' parsed from the pdftotext -layout rendering of pages 684-704, giving 499 words; the whole of Bull GCOS 7 Appendix A (PDF pp.611-626) scanned for each candidate.3. For a word absent from its appendix, looked for it as a keyword of a general format in the same manual, and accepted it only where the manual both shows it inside a Format and gives it its own syntax-element or phrase description.4. For the 47 switch names, found each family's documented range in a vendor manual, quoted the sentence, expanded the range and dropped everything outside it. gnucobol-guide.notes: The guide is under the GNU Free Documentation License 1.3. This record keeps the fact that it names each word and where, not any of its text. Confirmed against cobc (GnuCOBOL) 3.2.0 with -std=default. ORIGINS, as far as documents readable under their publishers' terms show. B-SHIFT-L, B-SHIFT-R, B-SHIFT-LC and B-SHIFT-RC are the boolean shift operators of ISO/IEC 1989:2023, and ACTIVATING, TOP-LEVEL, CURRENT, NESTED, STACK, ANUM, HEX, NAT, FLOAT-INFINITY, FLOAT-NOT-A-NUMBER and PHYSICAL are further 2023 vocabulary (MODULE-NAME arguments, CONVERT, the floating-point clauses, LENGTH); the guide lists them in its reserved-word table, several as reserved but not implemented, and the 2023 text itself is paywalled. IBM Enterprise COBOL 6.4 reserves B-AND, B-OR, B-XOR and B-NOT but no shift operator. COB-CRT-STATUS is GnuCOBOL's implicit register for a program without a CRT STATUS clause (X/Open and Micro Focus have the clause, not the register); the guide places it under 7.7 Special Registers, not in screenio.cpy, which holds the COB-SCR-* and COB-COLOR-* constants. MODULE-DATE, MODULE-FORMATTED-DATE, MODULE-PATH, MODULE-TIME, SUBSTITUTE and SUBSTITUTE-CASE are GnuCOBOL extensions; no other implementation readable here documents them. STDIN, STDOUT and STDERR are GnuCOBOL device names beside the SYSIN, SYSOUT, SYSERR and CONSOLE the other implementations share. NOTHING came with CALL ... RETURNING NOTHING in GnuCOBOL 2.2. NONNUMERIC is IBM's, from the generic suppression phrase XML GENERATE gained in Enterprise COBOL 5.2 and JSON GENERATE in 6.3; it is attested here from IBM's 6.4 Language Reference as well. PASCAL and STDCALL, until now attested by the Fujitsu NetCOBOL manual alone, are listed in the guide's table too. DROPPED: MODULE-NAME, which the guide lists as reserved but not implemented and cobc gives no role; and C, of WITH C LINKAGE (Fujitsu's calling-convention phrase), a single letter left out as X and Y were, since crediting it would hide a one-letter name a program never declared - the parser reads the phrase instead.

ibm-ec-zos-reserved.title: IBM Enterprise COBOL for z/OS, Version 6.4, Language Reference -- appendix "Reserved words" (form number SC27-8713-03, not attested in the fetched bytes)
ibm-ec-zos-reserved.method: curl -sS -L the topic URL to src/ibm-ec-zos-reserved-appendix.html (IBM Docs serves this appendix as raw server-rendered HTML; no JS needed). The page holds exactly one <table class="defaultstyle">. Split it into <tr> rows, then each row into cells with the regex <t[dh][^>]*>(.*?)</t[dh]>; every row has exactly 4 cells. Cell text = strip tags, html.unescape, map NBSP to space, collapse whitespace, strip. Row 1 is the header and is asserted to equal ['Word','Reserved','Standard only','Potential reserved words'], which pins the column order; the remaining 529 rows are data. Column 1 is the word cell, columns 2-4 are IBM's category marker columns holding either 'X' or NBSP -- so word cells are separated from marker cells by COLUMN POSITION (each cell's headers="rlres__entry__1..4" attribute independently confirms its column), never by guessing which token looks like a word. The literal 'X' of a marker column is therefore never eligible to become a word. Asserted invariant: each data row carries exactly one 'X' across the three marker columns, so no word falls in two IBM categories (529 X markers over 529 rows). A word cell is kept as a word only if it fully matches [A-Z][A-Z0-9-]*; the 14 cells that do not match are IBM's operator/punctuation rows, where the cell holds a symbol plus a prose gloss (e.g. '+ Arithmetic operator - unary plus or addition') -- these are quoted in notes and excluded from words, being reserved characters rather than words. 529 - 14 = 515 words, 0 duplicates. Every one of the 515 is then asserted to occur as a literal byte substring of the hashed file. Independent arithmetic cross-check against a raw-HTML tally: 529 X markers + 515 words = 1044 uppercase-ish tokens, matching exactly. Rebuild with bin/ibm_zos_reserved_build.py, whose asserts fail loudly if IBM changes the table shape.

iso-1989.title: ISO/IEC 1989, Information technology - Programming languages, their environments and system software interfaces - Programming language COBOL. Re-derived from the two public draft texts of the standard that are reachable without a paywall: (1) ISO/IEC FCD 1989:2001 (E), Final Committee Draft, working document ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 22/WG 4 N 0147, dated 2001-01-15, circulated by the SC 22 secretariat as SC 22 N 3204 - this is the draft of the edition published as ISO/IEC 1989:2002; and (2) ISO/IEC 1989:20xx CD 1.2 (E), Committee Draft International Standard, dated 2009-08-23, distributed as file std.zip by the INCITS PL22.4 (formerly J4) COBOL Task Group - this is a draft on the track to ISO/IEC 1989:2014. The official ISO previews of ISO/IEC 1989:2014 and ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (front matter only) were used to confirm clause numbering but contain no word lists.
iso-1989.publisher: ISO/IEC (JTC 1/SC 22/WG 4); the CD text as distributed by INCITS PL22.4 / J4
iso-1989.method: Located the documents first, then parsed them by glyph coordinates rather than by reading order. (1) Fetched the SC 22 public document register pages open/n2550..n4600 from open-std.org and grepped them for COBOL entries; N3204 is registered as "FCD Ballot on FCD 1989, Information Technology - Programming Languages - Cobol" (2001-01-18, distribution Open) and the file itself is served at https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/open/n3204.pdf (891 pages). The later COBOL entries in the register (N4561 FCD 1989 for the 2014 edition, N4562, N4403) are not served from open-std.org - every extension returns 404 - so the 2014 and 2023 texts are not there. (2) For a later draft, queried the Internet Archive CDX API for cobolstandard.info, the domain that hosted the INCITS J4 / PL22.4 COBOL Task Group document register until the domain lapsed, and found /j4/files/std.zip. The 2016-03-14 capture (identical by sha256 to the 2011-07-21 capture) contains one member, STD.BK.pdf, whose first page reads "ISO/IEC 1989:20xx CD 1.2 (E) ... Date: 2009-08-23 ... Document type: Committee Draft International Standard" (910 pages). (3) In each PDF, found the pages carrying 8.9 Reserved words, 8.10 Context-sensitive words, 8.11 Intrinsic function names and 8.12 Compiler-directive (reserved) words by searching page text, then measured the x-origin of every text span on those pages. Each list is a multi-column flow with two or three exact column origins (e.g. FCD pages 162-164 of the PDF at x=87.6/231.6/375.6, x=104.6/248.6/392.6, x=87.6/231.6/375.6). Harvested only spans whose x-origin is exactly a column origin; everything rejected was logged and inspected, and it is entirely running heads, folios, the clause heading and the lead-in sentence. Reconstructed the reading order as (column, y) and then verified the result by checking that the sequence is strictly ascending in ASCII order - a merged or dropped span breaks that invariant. The only violations were the document's own orderings (FLOAT-BINARY-7 before FLOAT-BINARY-16; END-IF before END-EVALUATE in 8.12; EOL/EOS before ENTRY-CONVENTION in 8.10) and the special-character words at the tail of each list. (4) Exception-names were read from Table 13 (FCD) and Table 14 (CD) by taking the leading EC-* token of each table line in the clause range; both results are strictly alphabetically ordered with no gaps. (5) Text for quoting and for the self-check was produced separately with poppler pdftotext -layout, an extractor independent of the coordinate parse used to build the lists. Scripts are in bin/ (flow.py, colmap.py, ecnames.py, build.py); all fetched bytes are in src/.

modern-vendors.title: Reserved-word appendices of six independent COBOL implementations: Veryant isCOBOL Evolve 2025 R1 Appendices, Appendix A 'isCOBOL Reserved Words'; Heirloom Computing Elastic COBOL Language Reference Manual Appendix, revision August 2012, Appendix A 'COBOL Reserved Words' and Appendix B 'Elastic COBOL Reserved Words'; Stratus VOS COBOL Language R010-03, Appendix A 'COBOL Reserved Words'; HP COBOL Manual for TNS and TNS/R Programs, part number 522555-006, Section 21 'Reserved Words'; Unisys COBOL ANSI-85 Programming Reference Manual Volume 1, Basic Implementation, form 8600 1518-307 (February 2003), Appendix B 'Reserved Words'; VSI COBOL Reference Manual, VSI COBOL Version 3.1-7 for OpenVMS, Appendix A 'VSI COBOL for OpenVMS Reserved Words'
modern-vendors.publisher: Veryant LLC; Heirloom Computing Inc.; Stratus Technologies; Hewlett-Packard (NonStop); Unisys Corporation; VMS Software Inc. (VSI)
modern-vendors.method:
curl (browser User-Agent) fetched each document into src/, sha256sum hashed it, and all parsing ran locally against those exact bytes via scripts left in bin/ under a modern-vendors- prefix. (1) Stratus VOS: the appendix body is a single 
 block, one word per line, lowercase, with a leading '*' marking implementation extensions; the parser strips tags, uppercases, removes the '*' marker and discards the operator rows that close the list. (2) Veryant isCOBOL: each word is its own 
CELL
 and only those cells were taken. That page renders COBOL hyphens as ASCII underscore 0x5F (END_ACCEPT, WORKING_STORAGE, I_O_CONTROL; only CODE-SET escaped the substitution, and no hyphenated form occurs anywhere on the page), so '_' was mapped back to '-'. Two further pages of the same documentation set were fetched as corroboration and spell WORKING-STORAGE, SPECIAL-NAMES, FILE-CONTROL, I-O-CONTROL and END-PERFORM with real hyphens. (3) Elastic COBOL: Appendix A (pp. 7-8) and Appendix B (pp. 9-12) are 4-column tables; the parser reads PyMuPDF word boxes, drops the running footer by y and the headings by font size (>=12pt), assigns each word to the nearest of the four most frequent x positions, sorts each column by y, then joins any token ending in '-' to the next token in the same column - which is what reassembles ALPHABETIC-LOWER, WORKING-STORAGE, COMPUTATIONAL-1-MVS and COMPUTATIONAL-2-REV. (4) HP NonStop: Section 21 is a single-column list on pp. 1161-1172; lines holding exactly one [A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+ token are kept, which excludes the multi-token running heads, footers and letter-index rows. The manual's own figure states All = new-COBOL + HP-only, and the extraction reproduces it: the 29 HP-only words come out as a proper subset of the 373. (5) Unisys: Appendix B, pp. 1293-1298, is a 3-column table beneath an intro paragraph, with '**' marking words new in ANSI-85 and a hanging indent on wrapped cells. Every text line containing a lowercase letter is discarded first - this removes the prose, headings and footers, and is what keeps ANSI-85 and ANSI-74 out of the word list - then the remaining words are bucketed into a band [col_x-3, col_x+30) so a hanging-indent continuation stays in its own column, joined on trailing '-', and stripped of '**'. (6) VSI COBOL: Appendix A is printed twice, as a 4-column table (pp. 525-529) and as a single-column list carrying the conditional markers (pp. 530-541). Both were parsed and unioned because each omits words the other holds: DYNAMIC, ORGANIZATION, OTHER, OTHERS, OUTPUT, OVERFLOW and OWNER appear only in the 4-column rendering, verified as exact tokens on pp. 526 and 528. U+2013 EN DASH stands in for the hyphen throughout and was normalised to '-', U+00A0 to space, and the '(S)' notation (DUPLICATE(S), HIGH-VALUE(S), LOW-VALUE(S), QUOTE(S)) was expanded into both the singular and the plural word. The six products' lists were then unioned, two single-document misspellings removed (see notes), and the result sorted. Finally every extracted word was re-checked against the bytes of its own source file with a regex tolerating whitespace after each hyphen (bin/modern-vendors-verify2.py); the per-product lists remain in bin/modern-vendors-*.txt.
